As enterprises rush to integrate artificial intelligence, choosing between a legacy services giant and a specialized software provider is a difficult task for investors. Should you buy International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) or Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS)?

International Business Machines is a leader in enterprise services, with a strong focus on hybrid cloud and consulting. In contrast, Synopsys provides the specialized software and intellectual property needed to design the chips powering modern computing. Both companies are central to the digital economy, yet they offer very different financial profiles and market exposures for you to consider.

The case for International Business Machines

International Business Machines focuses on providing software, consulting, and infrastructure solutions to a global client base. The company serves critical sectors like financial services and healthcare, helping them manage complex hybrid cloud environments. Its strategic ecosystem includes partners such as Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW), Salesforce (NYSE:CRM), Samsung Electronics, and SAP (NYSE:SAP). Additionally, it maintains unique long-term relationships, such as its partnership with the United States Tennis Association.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $67.5 billion, which was an increase of roughly 7.6% over the prior year. The company reported net income of approximately $10.6 billion for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of nearly 15.7%, a significant improvement over earlier years. These figures suggest that the transition toward higher-margin software and consulting services is having a tangible impact on the bottom line.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 2.1x, indicating a significant level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations using assets expected to be converted to cash within a year, was approximately 0.9x. For the fiscal year ended in December 2025, the company generated free cash flow of roughly $12.1 billion. This cash generation, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, supports its ability to fund operations and return capital to shareholders.

The case for Synopsys

In the competitive landscape of semiconductor stocks, Synopsys provides essential electronic design automation software and silicon intellectual property. Its tools are used by chip manufacturers and systems companies to design and test complex integrated circuits. The company has secured key relationships, including an intellectual property agreement with Amazon and a strategic partnership with OpenAI. Synopsys also utilizes a global network of channel partners to distribute its specialized engineering software to various vertical markets.

title: What Is The Case For Waiting On Rigetti Computing Stock?

Shares of Rigetti Computing (RGTI) closed at their lowest level in a year on October 30, having lost 71.5% over the past year against an 11.3% return for the S&P 500. Anyone buying at that price is still betting that the company can turn its Novera quantum computers into steady sales, and that its Cepheus-1-108Q system will reach management's accuracy aim by the end of 2026. After a fall that deep, is now still too early?

Rigetti Computing Is Still Priced Far Above Sales

On price alone, the fall has not made Rigetti cheap. Shares traded at 280.7 times the company's sales over the past twelve months at the October 30 close, compared with 3.2 times for the S&P 500. While that October 30 multiple marked a drop from 482.1 times sales at the end of June, the June valuation stood higher than at 13 of the 16 quarter ends since the third quarter of 2022.

The company is also losing money, shedding $97.2 million at the operating line on $13.4 million of sales in the twelve months to June. Because both earnings and operating cash flow were negative, neither provides a usable multiple. Rigetti did hold $394 million of cash and short-term investments at the end of June.

Sales have shown recent growth. Second-quarter revenue climbed 185.3% from a year earlier, an increase management attributed to on-premises Novera QPU sales. That growth covers only the first and second quarters. In each of the two preceding quarters, revenue fell from a year earlier.

What Rigetti Computing Expects By The End Of 2026

As of the August 6 call, Cepheus-1-108Q had not yet reached management's accuracy aim. The system ran at a median two-qubit gate fidelity, a measure of accuracy, of roughly 99.1%, while management aims for about 99.5% later in 2026.

On sales, management pointed to the fourth quarter. It still expects to count the $8.4 million C-DAC order for a 108-qubit system in India as revenue during that period, once the system is installed and accepted. Management also said revenue moves with the timing of system deliveries and government-funded projects. After that call, in August, Rigetti reorganized its leadership structure around customer deployments.

Analysts expect third-quarter revenue of about $3.75 million, which sits below the $5.14 million Rigetti reported for the second quarter. At today's multiple, the price appears to assume sales growth over several years, not in the third quarter.

title: Why Is Everyone Ignoring Omnicom Stock's High Cash Yield?

Why Is Everyone Ignoring Omnicom Stock's High Cash Yield?

Omnicom (OMC) stock offers a free cash flow yield of 12.9%, three times the 4.3% of the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high belongs either to a bargain or to a business investors expect to shrink. A year after buying Interpublic, Omnicom still has to show that its cash keeps coming and that it earns enough to pay for the deal's debt. So why do investors still pay so little for Omnicom's cash?

Omnicom Makes More Cash, But Owes Much More

Part of the answer is debt. Management said on its October 22 call that Omnicom took on about $3 billion of Interpublic's debt, and its total debt was $11.4 billion on September 30, 2026, against $7.07 billion a year earlier. Net of its cash, that debt equals 34% of Omnicom's market value. The cash yield is lower once that debt is counted as part of the price.

Omnicom's owners have a claim on the cash left after the lenders are paid, whether the company hands it out or holds it. That cash can support the share price over time, especially when it keeps rising.

Omnicom's cash has been rising. The company sells marketing services to clients such as Mercedes-Benz, and it spends little to keep that work running. Capital spending took 6.9% of its cash from operations over the last twelve months. Free cash flow for the twelve months to September 2026 was $2.86 billion, against $0.721 billion three years earlier, and it rose in each of those years. In fiscal Q3 2026, the latest quarter, free cash flow was $0.913 billion, against $0.438 billion in fiscal Q3 2025. The 2026 figures include Interpublic, which the earlier figures do not.

Why Do Investors Doubt Omnicom's Merged Business?

Investors appear wary because Omnicom's reported profit has shrunk since the merger. Its operating margin over the last twelve months was 6.6%, against 13.4% a year earlier. Those twelve months include the December 2025 quarter, when Omnicom reported an operating loss of $0.977 billion. Over the nine months from January to September 2026, the operating margin was 13.6%, slightly above the 13.4% of a year earlier.

The latest quarter looks better. In fiscal Q3 2026, Omnicom's operating margin was 15.4%, up from 13.1% in fiscal Q3 2025. Management put organic growth in the businesses it is keeping at 7.2% for the quarter, and said the company is on track to deliver $900 million of cost reductions in 2026.

So far, Omnicom earns enough to pay its lenders. Twelve-month operating income stood at 3.6 times its interest expense. Management expects net interest expense of just under $100 million in the December 2026 quarter, against $53.2 million a year earlier, and close to the $104 million of fiscal Q3 2026.
